name: Chapter 12: Ecosystem
description: Ecosystem structure, pond ecosystem, productivity, decomposition, energy flow, food chains, trophic levels and ecological pyramids

cards.definition: A functional unit of nature where organisms interact among themselves and with the physical environment
The biosphere: composite of all local ecosystems

cards.term: Two basic categories of ecosystems with examples?
cards.definition: Terrestrial: forest, grassland, desert. Aquatic: pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary.
Crop fields, aquarium
Identification and enumeration of plant and animal species of an ecosystem
Vertical distribution of species at different levels
Trees: top layer; shrubs: second; herbs and grasses: bottom

cards.text: Four functional aspects of an ecosystem: {{c1::productivity}}, {{c2::decomposition}}, {{c3::energy flow}}, {{c4::nutrient cycling}}.

cards.term: Why is a pond a good model ecosystem?
cards.definition: Fairly self-sustainable, simple, and shows all four functional aspects

Abiotic: Water with dissolved substances, bottom soil; sun, temperature, day-length; Autotrophs: Phytoplankton, algae, floating/submerged/marginal plants; Consumers: Zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms; Decomposers: Fungi, bacteria, flagellates (at the bottom)

cards.term: Direction of energy flow in an ecosystem?
cards.definition: Unidirectional towards higher trophic levels, with loss as heat
Abiotic (air, water, soil, climate) and biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers)

cards.term: Basic requirement for an ecosystem to function?
cards.definition: Constant input of solar energy
Amount of biomass/organic matter produced per unit area over time by plants during photosynthesis

cards.term: Units of primary production vs productivity?
cards.definition: Production: g m⁻² or kcal m⁻². Productivity (rate): g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.
Gross primary productivity: rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis
Net primary productivity = GPP − respiration losses (R)
\( NPP = GPP - R \)
Biomass available to heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers)
Rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers
Primary: by producers (photosynthesis). Secondary: by consumers.
Plant species, environmental factors, nutrient availability, photosynthetic capacity
About 170 billion tons (dry weight)
Only 55 billion tons despite covering ~70% of the surface
Light does not penetrate deep and nutrients (N, P) are limiting in open ocean
Light (also nutrients)
"Gross = Gross salary, Net = take-home": respiration is the tax the plant pays itself

cards.term: Why is the earthworm the "farmer’s friend"?
cards.definition: Breaks down complex organic matter and loosens the soil
Breakdown of complex organic matter into inorganic CO₂, water and nutrients by decomposers
Dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) and dead animal remains incl. faecal matter: raw material for decomposition
"Farmers Love Cows, Hens, Mangoes": Fragmentation, Leaching, Catabolism, Humification, Mineralisation
Detritivores (e.g. earthworm) break detritus into smaller particles
Water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and precipitate as unavailable salts
Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances

cards.term: Do decomposition steps happen in sequence?
cards.definition: No; all operate simultaneously on the detritus
Accumulation of dark, amorphous humus, highly resistant to microbes, decomposed extremely slowly

cards.term: Why is humus a nutrient reservoir?
cards.definition: It is colloidal
Release of inorganic nutrients by microbial degradation of humus
Largely oxygen-requiring
Slow: rich in lignin and chitin. Fast: rich in nitrogen and water-soluble sugars.

cards.term: Most important climatic factors for decomposition?
cards.definition: Temperature and soil moisture
Warm and moist favour; low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit → organic matter builds up

cards.term: Why do peat bogs and tundra accumulate organic matter? (intuition)
cards.definition: Cold and waterlogged (anaerobic): decomposers work very slowly
Earthworm
Production: inorganic → organic by producers. Decomposition: organic → inorganic by decomposers.
Litter: dead plant parts on the ground. Detritus: all dead plant and animal remains incl. faeces.

cards.term: Only ecosystem not dependent on the sun?
cards.definition: Deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystem

cards.term: What fraction of incident solar radiation is PAR? (Exercise 5)
cards.definition: Less than 50%

cards.term: What fraction of PAR do plants capture?
cards.definition: Only 2–10%

cards.term: Energy flow and the first law of thermodynamics?
cards.definition: Energy is not created; it flows unidirectionally from sun → producers → consumers

cards.term: Why do ecosystems obey the second law?
cards.definition: They need a constant energy supply to counter increasing disorder (entropy)

cards.term: Major producers in terrestrial vs aquatic ecosystems?
cards.definition: Terrestrial: herbaceous and woody plants. Aquatic: phytoplankton, algae, higher plants.
Interdependency: an animal feeds on a plant/animal and is food for another

cards.term: Where does the detritus food chain begin?
cards.definition: With death of an organism
Primary: eat producers (herbivores). Secondary: eat herbivores (primary carnivores). Tertiary: eat primary carnivores.
Insects, birds, mammals (land); molluscs (aquatic)
Grass (producer) → goat (primary consumer) → man (secondary consumer)

cards.term: What makes up the detritus food chain?
cards.definition: Decomposers (fungi and bacteria): saprotrophs that secrete enzymes to digest dead matter and absorb products

cards.term: Which chain dominates energy flow in water vs land?
cards.definition: Aquatic: grazing food chain. Terrestrial: detritus food chain carries much more energy.
GFC: starts with producers, sun-dependent. DFC: starts with dead organic matter, decomposers.
Natural interconnection of food chains; DFC organisms eaten by GFC animals, omnivores (cockroaches, crows)
Chain: single linear path. Web: interconnected chains.
An organism’s place in a food chain based on its source of nutrition
1st trophic level (producers): Phytoplankton, grass, trees; 2nd (herbivores): Zooplankton, grasshopper, cow; 3rd (carnivores): Birds, fishes, wolf; 4th (top carnivores): Man, lion

cards.term: Second trophic level in a lake (Exercise 3)?
cards.definition: Zooplankton

cards.term: What happens to energy at successive trophic levels?
cards.definition: It decreases; lost as heat at each step
Mass of living material at a trophic level at a particular time (biomass or number per unit area)

cards.term: Why is dry weight a better measure of biomass?
cards.definition: Water content varies and carries no energy; dry weight is accurate

cards.term: What is the 10 per cent law?
cards.definition: Only 10% of energy is transferred to the next trophic level

cards.term: Why are grazing food chains short? (intuition)
cards.definition: After 4–5 levels too little energy remains (10% × 10% × 10%…) to support another level

cards.term: Is there a limit on the detritus food chain?
cards.definition: Not in the same way; decomposers work on dead matter from all levels
Pyramid of number, biomass, energy

cards.term: What do base and apex represent?
cards.definition: Base: producers. Apex: top consumers.

cards.term: Grassland pyramid of numbers: producers vs top carnivores?
cards.definition: About 5,842,000 plants support only 3 top carnivores
P 809, PC 37, SC 11, TC 1.5 kg m⁻²

cards.term: Inverted pyramid of biomass: where and why?
cards.definition: Sea: small standing crop of phytoplankton (4) supports larger zooplankton (21)

cards.term: How can small phytoplankton biomass support larger consumers? (paradox)
cards.definition: Phytoplankton reproduce very fast (high turnover), so productivity is high though standing crop is small

cards.term: Pyramid of numbers for a single tree with insects and birds?
cards.definition: Inverted (one tree, many insects, fewer birds): spindle/inverted shape

cards.term: Pyramid of numbers in a tree-dominated ecosystem (Exercise 1b)?
cards.definition: Inverted

cards.term: Why is the pyramid of energy always upright?
cards.definition: Energy is always lost as heat at each transfer; it can never be inverted
1,000,000 J sunlight → P 10,000 J → PC 1000 J → SC 100 J → TC 10 J

cards.term: What % of sunlight do producers convert into NPP (Figure 12.4d)?
cards.definition: Only 1%

cards.term: Why must pyramid calculations include all organisms at a level?
cards.definition: Generalisations from a few individuals would be untrue

cards.term: Is a trophic level a species?
cards.definition: No; it is a functional level; a species can occupy more than one

cards.term: Example of a species at two trophic levels?
cards.definition: Sparrow: primary consumer eating seeds/fruits, secondary consumer eating insects/worms
Upright: broad base (most ecosystems). Inverted: narrow base (tree–insect numbers, sea biomass).
Ignore a species at two or more levels assume a simple chain, not a web give no place to saprophytes (decomposers)
Numbers, grassland: Upright; Numbers, single tree: Inverted; Biomass, land: Upright; Biomass, sea: Inverted; Energy, any: Always upright
